title: GPU-Native Operators in Ray Data | Anyscale
gist: Anyscale, collaborating with NVIDIA's cuDF team, has shipped two GPU-native features in Ray Data (Ray 2.58): cuDF as a first-class batch format for map_batches and a GPU-native shuffle built on RapidsMPF that moves data over RDMA/NVLink, bypassing the CPU and Ray object store. On fuzzy-deduplication benchmarks for foundation-model data curation (FineWeb 10BT), the GPU path delivered up to 15x speedups on hashing, 4x faster end-to-end runtime, and up to 3.1x better TCO than CPU clusters — though shuffle-heavy stages showed diminishing returns as GPU count grew.

themes.theme: GPU-native data processing lands in Ray Data

insights.claim: Ray Data historically treated GPUs only as a scheduling resource for user-defined functions, delegating actual GPU execution to libraries like PyTorch or JAX; as of Ray 2.58 it gains native GPU operators via cuDF batch-format support and a RapidsMPF-based GPU shuffle.
insights.speaker: Richard Liaw, Felix Cheung and Lee Yang
insights.so_what: AI data-curation pipelines are moving from CPU dataframes to GPU-native execution, expanding the addressable GPU workload beyond training/inference into data preprocessing.

insights.claim: Anyscale collaborated directly with the NVIDIA cuDF team to integrate GPU-based operators into Ray Data, claiming up to 3x better TCO versus CPU-based solutions on select data curation workloads.
insights.speaker: Richard Liaw, Felix Cheung and Lee Yang
insights.so_what: NVIDIA is seeding its CUDA-X software stack into open-source data engines, deepening ecosystem lock-in and giving GPU instances a cost-per-job argument even at higher hourly prices.
insights.quote: On select data curation workloads, these enhancements have enabled up to 3x better TCO compared to CPU-based solutions.

insights.claim: Ray Data's map_batches now accepts batch_format="cudf", handing UDFs a cudf.DataFrame with a Pandas-like API, and cuDF can be up to an order of magnitude faster and cheaper than CPU equivalents for compute-heavy operations.
insights.speaker: Richard Liaw, Felix Cheung and Lee Yang
insights.so_what: Drop-in Pandas-like GPU dataframes lower the switching cost from CPU to GPU pipelines — watch for demand shift from CPU-heavy to GPU data-processing instance fleets.
insights.locator: cuDF as a first-class batch format

insights.claim: The new GPU-native shuffle path built on RapidsMPF has ranks communicating directly over UCXX using RDMA or NVLink transports, bypassing both the CPU and the Ray object store entirely.
insights.speaker: Richard Liaw, Felix Cheung and Lee Yang
insights.so_what: GPU-to-GPU interconnect (NVLink/RDMA) becomes load-bearing for data processing, not just training — reinforces value of high-bandwidth networking in AI infrastructure buildouts.
insights.quote: Between ranks, shuffled data take advantage of high performance transports like RDMA or NVLink, skipping the CPU and Ray object store.

themes.theme: Benchmark economics: GPU beats CPU on TCO for data curation

insights.claim: On fuzzy deduplication of the FineWeb 10BT dataset, GPU-accelerated MinHash signature generation with cuDF ran roughly 15x faster than a Numpy CPU baseline consistently across 2, 4, and 8-node clusters (15.2x, 15.3x, 15.7x).
insights.speaker: Richard Liaw, Felix Cheung and Lee Yang
insights.so_what: Hash-heavy compute stages are near-ideal GPU workloads with linear scaling — the strongest leg of the GPU-for-data-processing thesis.

insights.claim: End-to-end, the GPU-accelerated dedup pipeline was 4x faster and 3.1x cheaper in TCO than the lowest-cost CPU configuration at 2 nodes ($0.69 vs $2.16), and delivered TCO and runtime improvements at every node scale tested (2.9x at 4 nodes, 2.2x at 8 nodes).
insights.speaker: Richard Liaw, Felix Cheung and Lee Yang
insights.so_what: GPU instances at ~27% higher hourly cost (g6.4xlarge $1.3232/hr vs m8id.4xlarge $1.04416/hr) still won on total cost — an argument that will pull data-curation spend onto GPU fleets.

insights.claim: The benchmark compared AWS m8id.4xlarge CPU instances (16 vCPUs, 64 GiB, $1.04416/hr) against g6.4xlarge GPU instances (16 vCPUs, 64 GiB, $1.3232/hr), meaning the GPU TCO win came from throughput, not cheaper hardware.
insights.speaker: Richard Liaw, Felix Cheung and Lee Yang
insights.so_what: TCO-per-job, not price-per-hour, is becoming the deciding metric for AI data infrastructure purchasing — favors GPU utilization plays over commodity CPU compute.

themes.theme: Scaling limits: shuffle-bound stages hit diminishing returns

insights.claim: In shuffle-intensive grouping and connected-components stages, GPU speedup over CPU shrank as the cluster grew — 3.0x at 2 nodes, 2.4x at 4, and just 1.5x at 8 — because adding GPUs adds communication overhead.
insights.speaker: Richard Liaw, Felix Cheung and Lee Yang
insights.so_what: Communication overhead, not raw compute, is the binding constraint on scaling GPU data processing — supports the case for interconnect/networking vendors and right-sized (smaller) GPU clusters per job.
insights.quote: Since these stages are shuffle intensive, adding more GPUs adds more communication overhead.

insights.claim: For the FineWeb 10BT dedup workload, 2 GPUs was the cost-optimal cluster size; the dataset was likely too small to exploit 8 GPUs, so throwing more accelerators at a fixed-size job actively erodes cost savings.
insights.speaker: Richard Liaw, Felix Cheung and Lee Yang
insights.so_what: GPU right-sizing per dataset matters — efficiency tooling and schedulers that match cluster size to workload will capture value; naive GPU scale-out wastes spend.
insights.quote: For this particular dataset and workload, 2 GPUs was optimal, so the dataset was likely too small to take advantage of all 8 GPUs.

themes.theme: Roadmap: operator fusion and GPU-resident pipelines

insights.claim: Anyscale says current results are far from the performance ceiling: fusing sequential cuDF and RapidsMPF operators to keep data resident in GPU memory — avoiding host-to-device round trips — is expected to deliver a step-change improvement.
insights.speaker: Richard Liaw, Felix Cheung and Lee Yang
insights.so_what: The GPU data-processing TCO gap vs CPU should widen from here — the 3x figure is a floor, not a ceiling; watch subsequent Ray releases for fusion benchmarks.
insights.quote: operator fusion between sequential operators that use cuDF and RapidsMPF will provide a significant step change in performance

insights.claim: GPU shuffle in Ray Data is experimental as of Ray 2.58, with planned extension to the preprocessor API so feature-engineering pipelines also pick up the GPU path — signaling expansion beyond LLM data curation into classical ML feature engineering.
insights.speaker: Richard Liaw, Felix Cheung and Lee Yang
insights.so_what: The feature is early-stage; adoption risk exists, but the direction of travel is more of the data stack migrating onto GPUs — incremental demand for GPU capacity.

insights.claim: Fuzzy document deduplication via MinHash-LSH is described as a standard workload for foundation-model training data curation, making it a repeatable, high-volume GPU demand driver rather than a one-off benchmark.
insights.speaker: Richard Liaw, Felix Cheung and Lee Yang
insights.so_what: Every frontier-model training run needs data dedup at scale — a recurring compute cost center where GPU-native tooling now claims a 3x cost edge.
